'''An Euclidean circle''' is a [[circle]] in the [[Euclidean space#Special_Euclidean_spaces|Euclidean plane]].

[[File:Circle-O-r.svg]]

== Formal definition ==

Let $\mathbb{E}^2$ be an [[Euclidean space#Special_Euclidean_spaces|Euclidean plane]].

$$
\text{Circle}(\vec{c},r)=\{\vec{x}\in\mathbb{E}^2:\|\vec{x}-\vec{c}\|=r,\,  r>0, \vec c \in \mathbb{E}^2\}
$$

== Cartesian coordinate description ==

Let $X,C \in \mathbb{E}^2$ be points in an [[Euclidean space#Special_Euclidean_spaces|Euclidean plane]].

Let
$$
\vec{x}=(x,y),\quad \vec{c}=(c_1,c_2)
$$

be their position vectors, then

$$
\vec{x}\in\text{Circle}(\vec{c},r)\iff (x-c_1)^2+(y-c_2)^2=r^2
$$

[[File:Circle-cartesian-coordinate.svg|center]]

== Properties ==

=== $s=r\theta$ ===

[[File:Angle and arc length.png]]

{{Hidden proof}}
By definition of [[radian]],$\theta=1 \ \mathrm{rad}$ \iff s=r$

Since an Euclidean circle is symmetric according to any line passing through its center, putting two arcs of $1 \ \mathrm{rad}$ next to each other constructs an arc of $2\ \mathrm{rad}$ and a corresponding central angle of $2 \ \mathrm{rad}$, putting three arcs of $1 \ \mathrm{rad}$ next to each other constructs an arc of $2\ \mathrm{rad}$ and a corresponding central angle of $2 \ \mathrm{rad}$, so on so forth.

[[File:Circle-arc-addition-radians.svg|center]]

The logic also works in division. Dividing an arc of $1 \ \mathrm{rad}$ in two produces two arcs of $\frac{1}{2}\ \mathrm{rad}$ and corresponding central angles of $\frac{1}{2} \ \mathrm{rad}$ each, dividing an arc of $1 \ \mathrm{rad}$ in three produces three arcs of $\frac{1}{3}\ \mathrm{rad}$ and corresponding [[circle#Angles|central angles]] of $\frac{1}{3} \ \mathrm{rad}$ each, so on so forth.

[[File:Circle-arc-division-radians.svg|center]]

Therefore, it can be concluded: 

$$
s \propto \theta
$$

Now, since all Euclidean circles are geometrically similar, any [[circle#Areas|sector]] of equal central angle must be similar. i.e.,

$$
\frac{s_1}{s_2}=\frac{r_1}{r_2}
$$

We conclude therefore

$$
s \propto r
$$

Now, since
$$
s \propto \theta \land s \propto \theta
\Rightarrow s = kr\theta,\, k \in \mathbb{R} \\
$$

Insert $r=1,s=1,\theta=1, hence $k=1$.

i.e.,
$$
s=r\theta
$$

{{End hidden}}
